Analysis of Opinions.new: \item \textbf{A Targeted Statute That Failed \textit{Nixon}'s Test:} The D.C. Circuit applied \textit{Nixon} in \href{https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/351/1198/525998/}{\textit{Foretich v.\ United States}}, 351 F.3d 1198 (D.C. Cir.\ 2003).

Analysis of Opinions.src: There, Congress passed the Elizabeth Morgan Act---narrowly drafted so it applied only to a single notorious D.C. custody dispute---stripping Dr. Eric Foretich of parental visitation rights without a judicial finding of abuse. Applying \textit{Nixon}, the D.C. Circuit invalidated the statute as an unconstitutional bill of attainder: unlike the PRMPA's compensated archival custody, the Act imposed a severe, permanent deprivation of parental rights disproportionate to any nonpunitive purpose (failing the functional test) and rested on legislative condemnation of Foretich as an abuser (failing the motivational test).

Congress promptly enacted the Presidential Records Act of 1978, 44 U.S.C. \S\S~2201--2209, vesting public ownership of official presidential records in the United States. Decades later, \textit{Nixon}'s rule that an incumbent President's waiver of executive privilege outweighs a former President's objection proved decisive in \textit{Trump v. Thompson}, 20 F.4th 10 (D.C. Cir. 2021), \textit{stay denied}, 595 U.S. \_\_\_ (2022), permitting the National Archives to release January 6 White House records to Congress.

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (No Bill of Attainder): A Procurement Ban Naming One Company.}

Examples: Future Applications.src: Suppose Congress enacts a statute naming ``Apex AI Corp.'' and (a) prohibiting federal agencies from contracting with Apex due to documented foreign-intelligence vulnerabilities
provision (a) likely survives all three punishment prongs as prophylactic procurement regulation

Examples: Future Applications.new: : declining to buy from a vendor is not a traditional attainder sanction, the ban reasonably serves the nonpunitive goal of protecting federal systems, and a record of documented security risks shows regulatory concern rather than legislative condemnation. Like Nixon, Apex may be a legitimate class of one if it alone presents the identified risk.

\item \textbf{Same-Side (No Bill of Attainder): Securing One Official's Records.} After a former Cabinet secretary leaves office, Congress learns that she conducted official business on a private email server and that her personal attorney plans to delete messages. Congress passes a statute naming her and directing the National Archives to take custody of the server, have career archivists separate official from personal messages, return personal messages to her, and pay just compensation for any property taken. As in \textit{Nixon}, she is a legitimate class of one because only her records face imminent destruction; custody and screening are not traditional punishments; the statute furthers the nonpunitive goal of preserving public records; and the compensation and return provisions negate any inference of punitive confiscation.

Examples: Future Applications.new: , much as the Elizabeth Morgan Act failed in \textit{Foretich}. Unlike the PRMPA, which provided just compensation and served evidence-preservation goals, the forfeiture is a severe deprivation that does nothing to address the security risk and rests on legislative condemnation.

\item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Separation-of-Powers Problem): Congress Takes the Records Itself.} Congress passes a statute transferring custody of a departing President's records to a House committee, which may review and publish any record it chooses, including privileged national-security advice. The incumbent President, who supports the outgoing President's privilege claims, objects. \textit{Nixon} upheld the PRMPA because the records stayed under Executive Branch control, screening was done by career archivists, Congress received no privileged access, and the incumbent supported the law. Each of those features is missing here. A court applying \textit{Nixon}'s disruption test would likely find that the statute prevents the Executive Branch from protecting confidential communications without an overriding need to justify it.

Examples: Future Applications.src: Suppose a newly elected President waives executive privilege over a predecessor's candid Oval Office national-security memos so a congressional committee can publish them, despite no active criminal trial or pending legislation. Students should analyze whether \textit{Nixon}'s diminished-weight rule for former Presidents (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/433/425/}{433 U.S. at 449}) controls, or whether Justice Blackmun's hostile-transition warning and modern Article II formalism (\textit{Trump v. Mazars}; \textit{Trump v. United States}) demand heightened judicial scrutiny.

Examples: Future Applications.new: The incumbent's support favors disclosure under \textit{Nixon}, but unlike in \textit{Nixon}, publication rather than archival screening is at stake and no evidentiary need is present, so the outcome is genuinely uncertain.
